title: Motion Graphs
learning_goal: Interpret position-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs and connect each graph to an object's motion.

stages.title: 1. Understand the idea
stages.content: Motion describes how an object's position changes over time. On a position-time graph, time is on the horizontal axis and position is on the vertical axis. The slope tells how quickly position changes.

stages.title: 2. Read a position-time graph
stages.content: A horizontal line means the object is at rest. A straight line sloping upward means constant positive velocity. A straight line sloping downward means constant negative velocity. A steeper line means a greater speed.

stages.title: 3. Worked example
stages.content: A student moves from 0 m to 12 m in 4 s. Change in position = 12 m. Change in time = 4 s. Average velocity = Δx/Δt = 12/4 = 3 m/s.

stages.title: 4. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A car moves from 5 m to 25 m in 5 s. What is its average velocity?
stages.hint: Start by finding the change in position: 25 − 5.
stages.alternate_explanation: Think of velocity as the slope of a position-time graph: rise over run, or change in position divided by change in time.

stages.title: 5. Velocity-time graphs
stages.content: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity. An upward slope means positive acceleration. A downward slope means velocity is decreasing.

stages.title: 6. Acceleration-time graphs
stages.content: A horizontal line above zero means constant positive acceleration. A horizontal line below zero means constant negative acceleration. A line at zero means no acceleration, even though the object may still be moving.

stages.title: 7. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, explain motion from all three graph types, calculate velocity from position-time slope, calculate acceleration from velocity change, and match a motion description to the correct graph.
